extracted.intended_audience: USPTO Office personnel (patent examiners), patent practitioners/prosecutors
extracted.subtask_description: Office guidelines for determining and documenting obviousness rejections under 35 U.S.C. 103 (including post-KSR principles). Provides the factual inquiries, search guidance, permissible rationales, handling of applicant replies and rebuttal evidence, and examples of supporting reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham factual inquiries
rubrics_metrics.description: The objective analysis for determining obviousness is based on the factual inquiries set forth in Graham v. John Deere Co.: (A) determining the scope and content of the prior art; (B) ascertaining the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art; and (C) resolving the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art. Objective (secondary) evidence (commercial success, long-felt need, failure of others, unexpected results) must also be evaluated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These factors define the inquiry and must be analyzed in each case. Secondary considerations may be included in the specification, accompany the application, or be provided timely during prosecution. The weight of any objective evidence is case-by-case and presentation of evidence is not dispositive by itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Articulation of factual findings and reasoned rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel, acting as factfinders, must record findings of fact about the state of the art and teachings of references relied upon and provide an explanation supporting an obviousness rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The written record should contain explicit factual findings (including how a person of ordinary skill would have understood the prior art) and the rationale(s) tying those facts to a legal conclusion of obviousness. Rejections cannot be sustained by conclusory statements; examiners must articulate reasoning with a rational underpinning (KSR; In re Kahn). Clear findings enable applicant response and promote prompt resolution. Failure to state reasons may justify traverse; examiners may repeat and make final if traverse is not substantive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining the scope and content of the prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Obtain a thorough understanding of the invention by reading the specification and claims and determine the scope of the claimed invention by giving the claims the 'broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification.' Then determine what to search for and where to search.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read the specification and claims (see MPEP § 904 and § 2111). The search should cover the claimed subject matter and disclosed features that might reasonably be expected to be claimed. While a rejection need not be based on a teaching/suggestion to combine, a preferred search should seek references that provide such teaching/suggestion if they exist. Prior art includes references in the inventor's field or art reasonably pertinent to the problem addressed (analogous art). Prior art from other fields can be considered when variations would have been predictable to a person of ordinary skill (KSR). See MPEP §§ 901–904, 2141.01(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: What to search for and where to search (search strategy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Search should cover claimed subject matter and disclosed features that might be claimed; search locations should follow general search guidelines and include analogous art and other reasonably pertinent fields.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow MPEP § 904 and § 904.03. For 35 U.S.C. 103 prior art can be in the inventor’s field or another reasonably pertinent field (analogous art). Continue to seek references that (if present) provide a teaching, suggestion, or motivation to combine references, though such explicit teaching is not always required for a proper rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ascertaining differences between the claimed invention and prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpret claim language (see MPEP § 2111) and consider the invention and the prior art as a whole to identify differences between claim limitations and prior art disclosures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All claim limitations must be considered; determine what differences remain once prior art is applied. Differences alone do not establish nonobviousness — examiner must explain why those differences would or would not have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in view of the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolving the level of ordinary skill in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: An obviousness rejection should include, explicitly or implicitly, an indication of the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art. Factors include type of problems in the art, prior art solutions, rapidity of innovation, sophistication of the technology, and educational level of active workers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every factor need not be present and one or more may predominate (In re GPAC). A POSITA is a person of ordinary creativity (not an automaton) and may fit teachings together like puzzle pieces (KSR). Office personnel may rely on their own technical expertise; examiners are considered persons of scientific competence and familiar with skill level in the art. See MPEP § 2141.03 for implicit indication guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible rationales for finding obviousness (including examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Graham factual inquiries indicate obviousness, examiners may rely on several rationales — TSM is one but others are valid. Examples include (A) combining prior art elements by known methods to yield predictable results; (B) simple substitution of one known element for another to obtain predictable results; (C) using a known technique to improve similar devices in the same way; (D) applying a known technique to a known device ready for improvement to yield predictable results; (E) 'obvious to try' when choosing from a finite number of identified, predictable solutions with a reasonable expectation of success; (F) recognizing that work in one field may prompt predictable variations for another field; (G) some teaching/suggestion/motivation in the prior art to modify or combine references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This list is not exhaustive. The key is clear articulation of why the claimed invention would have been obvious. See MPEP § 2143 and § 2144 for examples and illustrations. Rationales must connect the facts to the legal conclusion and avoid conclusory generalizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching-suggestion-motivation (TSM) approach — valid but not rigid
rubrics_metrics.description: TSM may be used as a rationale for obviousness where appropriate, but post-KSR examiners should not apply TSM in an overly rigid or formalistic way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: KSR recognized TSM captured a helpful insight but rejected rigid application that precludes common-sense reasoning. Examiners may use TSM where present; absence of an explicit TSM in the prior art does not preclude an obviousness finding if other reasoned rationales exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of common sense and general knowledge in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners may invoke common sense or general knowledge to supply limitations or support a rationale for obviousness, but such use must be supported by evidence and a reasoned explanation, particularly where the missing limitation is central to the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common-sense reasoning cannot be merely conclusory; it must be supported by record evidence or a reasoned explanation (DyStar; Arendi). Particular care is required when the missing limitation goes to the heart of the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant reply requirements under 37 CFR 1.111(b)
rubrics_metrics.description: Once an obviousness rejection is made with factual findings and rationale, the burden shifts to the applicant to show error in the findings or otherwise show nonobviousness. 37 CFR 1.111(b) requires the applicant to distinctly and specifically point out supposed errors and reply to every ground of rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An effective traverse must include a reasoned statement explaining why the Office erred as to the factual findings. Mere assertions (e.g., 'no prima facie case' or 'reliance on common knowledge unsupported by documentary evidence') without substantive explanation are inadequate. If applicant's reply is inadequate, the examiner may repeat the rejection and make the next action final (see MPEP § 706.07(a)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of applicant’s rebuttal evidence and re-evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel must consider all timely rebuttal evidence when reevaluating an obviousness determination and should reconsider initial findings in view of the entire record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rebuttal evidence may include secondary considerations or arguments demonstrating e.g. (A) that a POSITA could not combine elements due to technical difficulties; (B) the combination does more than the separate functions of elements; or (C) the claimed combination produced unexpected results. After rebuttal, examiners should review all rejections and proposed rejections for continued viability and clearly communicate findings and conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary considerations (objective indicia) as part of obviousness analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of secondary considerations — commercial success, long-felt but unsolved needs, failure of others, unexpected results — is relevant and must be evaluated and weighed on a case-by-case basis as objective evidence bearing on obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secondary considerations can be presented in the specification, on filing, or later in prosecution. Their presence does not automatically determine obviousness; examiners must articulate factual findings and account for such evidence when reaching or reaffirming an obviousness conclusion (Graham; In re Piasecki; In re Eli Lilly).
